CHAPTER XX

Those in front had spread the news before us. We found the servants in
a state of panic. As we passed my lady’s door, it was thrown open
violently from the inner side. My mistress came out among us (with Mr.
Franklin following, and trying vainly to compose her), quite beside
herself with the horror of the thing.

“You are answerable for this!” she cried out, threatening the Sergeant
wildly with her hand. “Gabriel! give that wretch his money—and release
me from the sight of him!”

The Sergeant was the only one among us who was fit to cope with
her—being the only one among us who was in possession of himself.

“I am no more answerable for this distressing calamity, my lady, than
you are,” he said. “If, in half an hour from this, you still insist on
my leaving the house, I will accept your ladyship’s dismissal, but not
your ladyship’s money.”

It was spoken very respectfully, but very firmly at the same time—and
it had its effect on my mistress as well as on me. She suffered Mr.
Franklin to lead her back into the room. As the door closed on the two,
the Sergeant, looking about among the women-servants in his observant
way, noticed that while all the rest were merely frightened, Penelope
was in tears. “When your father has changed his wet clothes,” he said
to her, “come and speak to us, in your father’s room.”

Before the half-hour was out, I had got my dry clothes on, and had lent
Sergeant Cuff such change of dress as he required. Penelope came in to
us to hear what the Sergeant wanted with her. I don’t think I ever felt
what a good dutiful daughter I had, so strongly as I felt it at that
moment. I took her and sat her on my knee and I prayed God bless her.
She hid her head on my bosom, and put her arms round my neck—and we
waited a little while in silence. The poor dead girl must have been at
the bottom of it, I think, with my daughter and with me. The Sergeant
went to the window, and stood there looking out. I thought it right to
thank him for considering us both in this way—and I did.

People in high life have all the luxuries to themselves—among others,
the luxury of indulging their feelings. People in low life have no such
privilege. Necessity, which spares our betters, has no pity on _us_. We
learn to put our feelings back into ourselves, and to jog on with our
duties as patiently as may be. I don’t complain of this—I only notice
it. Penelope and I were ready for the Sergeant, as soon as the Sergeant
was ready on his side. Asked if she knew what had led her
fellow-servant to destroy herself, my daughter answered (as you will
foresee) that it was for love of Mr. Franklin Blake. Asked next, if she
had mentioned this notion of hers to any other person, Penelope
answered, “I have not mentioned it, for Rosanna’s sake.” I felt it
necessary to add a word to this. I said, “And for Mr. Franklin’s sake,
my dear, as well. If Rosanna _has_ died for love of him, it is not with
his knowledge or by his fault. Let him leave the house today, if he
does leave it, without the useless pain of knowing the truth.” Sergeant
Cuff said, “Quite right,” and fell silent again; comparing Penelope’s
notion (as it seemed to me) with some other notion of his own which he
kept to himself.

At the end of the half-hour, my mistress’s bell rang.

On my way to answer it, I met Mr. Franklin coming out of his aunt’s
sitting-room. He mentioned that her ladyship was ready to see Sergeant
Cuff—in my presence as before—and he added that he himself wanted to
say two words to the Sergeant first. On our way back to my room, he
stopped, and looked at the railway time-table in the hall.

“Are you really going to leave us, sir?” I asked. “Miss Rachel will
surely come right again, if you only give her time?”

“She will come right again,” answered Mr. Franklin, “when she hears
that I have gone away, and that she will see me no more.”

I thought he spoke in resentment of my young lady’s treatment of him.
But it was not so. My mistress had noticed, from the time when the
police first came into the house, that the bare mention of him was
enough to set Miss Rachel’s temper in a flame. He had been too fond of
his cousin to like to confess this to himself, until the truth had been
forced on him, when she drove off to her aunt’s. His eyes once opened
in that cruel way which you know of, Mr. Franklin had taken his
resolution—the one resolution which a man of any spirit _could_ take—to
leave the house.

What he had to say to the Sergeant was spoken in my presence. He
described her ladyship as willing to acknowledge that she had spoken
over-hastily. And he asked if Sergeant Cuff would consent—in that
case—to accept his fee, and to leave the matter of the Diamond where
the matter stood now. The Sergeant answered, “No, sir. My fee is paid
me for doing my duty. I decline to take it, until my duty is done.”

“I don’t understand you,” says Mr. Franklin.

“I’ll explain myself, sir,” says the Sergeant. “When I came here, I
undertook to throw the necessary light on the matter of the missing
Diamond. I am now ready, and waiting to redeem my pledge. When I have
stated the case to Lady Verinder as the case now stands, and when I
have told her plainly what course of action to take for the recovery of
the Moonstone, the responsibility will be off my shoulders. Let her
ladyship decide, after that, whether she does, or does not, allow me to
go on. I shall then have done what I undertook to do—and I’ll take my
fee.”

In those words Sergeant Cuff reminded us that, even in the Detective
Police, a man may have a reputation to lose.

The view he took was so plainly the right one, that there was no more
to be said. As I rose to conduct him to my lady’s room, he asked if Mr.
Franklin wished to be present. Mr. Franklin answered, “Not unless Lady
Verinder desires it.” He added, in a whisper to me, as I was following
the Sergeant out, “I know what that man is going to say about Rachel;
and I am too fond of her to hear it, and keep my temper. Leave me by
myself.”

I left him, miserable enough, leaning on the sill of my window, with
his face hidden in his hands and Penelope peeping through the door,
longing to comfort him. In Mr. Franklin’s place, I should have called
her in. When you are ill-used by one woman, there is great comfort in
telling it to another—because, nine times out of ten, the other always
takes your side. Perhaps, when my back was turned, he did call her in?
In that case it is only doing my daughter justice to declare that she
would stick at nothing, in the way of comforting Mr. Franklin Blake.

In the meantime, Sergeant Cuff and I proceeded to my lady’s room.

At the last conference we had held with her, we had found her not over
willing to lift her eyes from the book which she had on the table. On
this occasion there was a change for the better. She met the Sergeant’s
eye with an eye that was as steady as his own. The family spirit showed
itself in every line of her face; and I knew that Sergeant Cuff would
meet his match, when a woman like my mistress was strung up to hear the
worst he could say to her.

[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"What's the matter, master?" said I.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

The rumors had preceded us, spreading like wildfire through the corridors before we even reached the threshold. Upon entering, we found the household servants convulsing in a collective panic, a chaotic tableau of fear. As we approached my lady's chamber, the door flew open with violent urgency from within. My mistress emerged amidst the throng, trailed closely by Mr. Franklin, who strove in vain to compose her fraying composure. She was utterly undone by the sheer horror of the revelation.

"You are answerable for this!" she screamed, brandishing her hand in a wild, accusing gesture toward the Sergeant. "Gabriel! Give that wretch his money—and release me from the sight of him!"

Among the trembling group, the Sergeant alone possessed the fortitude to stand firm, being the sole individual capable of meeting her fury without flinching. "I am no more answerable for this distressing calamity, my lady, than you are," he replied. His tone was wrapped in profound respect yet cut with unyielding steel. "Should you still insist on my departure from this house within half an hour, I shall accept your ladyship's dismissal, but I most certainly shall not accept your ladyship's money."

The words landed with the weight of a gavel strike, affecting both my mistress and myself. She relented, allowing Mr. Franklin to guide her back into the sanctuary of the room. As the door sealed shut behind them, the Sergeant turned his observant gaze upon the cluster of female servants. While the others trembled in mere fright, he noted that Penelope was weeping openly.

"When your father has changed his wet clothes," he instructed her gently, "come and speak to us, in your father's room."

Before the allotted half-hour elapsed, I had donned my dry garments and provided the Sergeant with the fresh attire he required. Penelope entered then, summoned to hear the purpose of his summons. Never before had I felt the depth of my filial devotion so acutely as in that instant. I drew her close, seating her upon my knee, and implored God to bless her. She buried her face in my bosom, wrapping her arms tightly around my neck, and together we waited in a heavy, shared silence. In my heart, I believed the poor dead girl, Rosanna, lay at the root of this tragedy, alongside my daughter and myself.

The Sergeant moved to the window, standing sentinel as he gazed outward. I deemed it fitting to express my gratitude for his consideration of our plight, and I did so. There exists a peculiar luxury reserved for those of high station—the privilege of indulging raw emotion. For those of lower birth, necessity dictates otherwise; compassion is withheld from us. We are taught to suppress our feelings, to internalize our grief, and to march onward with our duties as patiently as possible. I make no complaint of this harsh reality; I merely observe it.

Soon, both Penelope and the Sergeant were prepared. When questioned regarding what motive might have driven her fellow servant to such a fatal act, my daughter answered—as one might predict—that it stemmed from her love for Mr. Franklin Blake. Next, asked if she had confided this suspicion to anyone else, Penelope replied, "I have not mentioned it, for Rosanna's sake."

I felt compelled to interject. "And for Mr. Franklin's sake, my dear, as well," I added softly. "If Rosanna *did* perish for love of him, it was neither with his knowledge nor by his fault. Should he depart this house today, let him do so without the useless agony of bearing the truth."

Sergeant Cuff nodded in agreement, "Quite right," before falling silent again, seemingly weighing Penelope's confession against some private hypothesis of his own.

At the stroke of the half-hour, my mistress's bell rang. En route to answer it, I encountered Mr. Franklin emerging from his aunt's sitting-room. He informed me that her ladyship was ready to receive the Sergeant, in my presence as previously arranged, and added that he desired a brief word with the officer first. Returning to my quarters, he paused to examine the railway timetable hanging in the hall.

"Are you truly intending to leave us, sir?" I asked. "Miss Rachel will surely recover if you simply grant her time?"

"She will come right again," Mr. Franklin answered, his voice devoid of hope, "once she realizes I have departed, and that she will never see me again."

I initially interpreted his words as a reaction to the young lady's recent treatment of him, but my assessment proved mistaken. From the moment the police arrived, my mistress had observed that the mere mention of his name ignited Miss Rachel's temper into a blaze. Too devoted to his cousin to admit this to himself until the truth forced its way upon him, he had retreated to his aunt's residence. Now, with eyes opened to a cruel clarity—a transformation familiar to those who know him—Mr. Franklin had made his resolve. It was the singular decision a man of spirit could make: to withdraw.

What he intended to say to the Sergeant was delivered in my presence. He described her ladyship as acknowledging that she had spoken too hastily. He then asked if the Sergeant would consent, under these circumstances, to accept his fee and leave the matter of the Diamond exactly as it stood.

"No, sir," the Sergeant replied flatly. "My fee is earned for performing my duty. I decline to accept payment until that duty is fully discharged."

"I do not understand you," Mr. Franklin said, perplexed.

"I shall explain, sir," the Sergeant continued. "Upon arriving here, I undertook to shed the necessary light upon the disappearance of the Diamond. I am now ready, and waiting, to fulfill my pledge. Once I have presented the current state of the case to Lady Verinder and clearly outlined the course of action required to recover the Moonstone, the burden of responsibility shall fall entirely upon her shoulders. Only then, after she decides whether to permit me to continue or cease, shall I consider my undertaking complete—and only then shall I claim my fee."

In those precise words, Sergeant Cuff reminded us that even within the ranks of the Detective Police, a man possesses a reputation to safeguard. His stance was undeniably correct, leaving no room for further debate. Rising to escort him to my lady's room, he inquired if Mr. Franklin wished to accompany us.

"Not unless Lady Verinder desires it," Mr. Franklin answered. Then, lowering his voice to a whisper as I followed the Sergeant out, he confessed, "I know what that man is about to say concerning Rachel; and I am too fond of her to listen, lest I lose my temper. Leave me to myself."

I departed, finding him miserably leaning against the window sill, his face concealed in his hands, while Penelope peered through the doorway, yearning to offer solace. Had I been in his position, I would have summoned her immediately. When one is mistreated by a woman, there is immense comfort in voicing the grievance to another, for nine times out of ten, the listener will take your side. Perhaps, while my back was turned, he did call her in? If so, it is only fair to declare that Penelope would stop at nothing to comfort Mr. Franklin Blake.

This time, however, a marked improvement was evident. She met the Sergeant's gaze with a steadiness that mirrored his own. A fierce family spirit illuminated every line of her face, and I knew that Sergeant Cuff would find his equal when a woman of my mistress's caliber was primed to endure the harshest truths.
